catalog_quote: Hayward (1982) described it as an accentual language, with an accent realized as a heightened pitch. Ford (1990) «feel[s] that loudness, rather than heightened pitch … is the principle exponent of stress.» She adds, however, that «[t]hough rare, there is a downward gliding tone which seems to be contrastive and which occurs only on stressed syllables.» In my analysis, based on data collected in Addis Ababa and Amaaro-Keele in May 2005, and in Addis Ababa in February, November/December 2006, and November/December 2007, Koorete is not a stress or accent language. It has two distinctive word level tones, a rising tone and a falling tone, marked in the following minimal pairs with an acute accent (´) and a grave accent (`), respectively, on the first vowel letter in a word ... ʔáaʃ'e v ‘curse’ ʔàaʃ'e v ‘scratch’ k'áme v ‘speak angrily’ k'àme v ‘become evening’ s'óome v ‘throw’ s'òome v ‘fast’ The rising tone is realized as a pitch rising throughout the word. Before a pause, the last syllable has a low tone (in Koorete, all non-clitic words are polysyllabic). The falling tone is realized as a slightly falling pitch throughout the word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Theil (most recent first-hand phonological analysis): Koorete has no word stress or accent; each word carries one of two lexical word-level tonal melodies, rising (pitch rises across the word, final syllable low before pause) or falling (slightly falling pitch across the word), contrasting in minimal pairs such as k'áme 'speak angrily' vs k'àme 'become evening'. Earlier accounts disagree: Hayward 1982 treats it as a pitch accent ('accentual') language, Ford 1990 as having stress cued by loudness, and Azeb Amha 2007 (EAE 3:429-430) as a 'tone-accent language' with two tones (H, L) where H is restricted in its occurrence within the word; none of the accessible texts states a fixed syllable position for the accent/H.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any accessible source.
new_statements.exceptions: Theil: before pause the last syllable of a rising-tone word is low; all non-clitic words are polysyllabic. Ford (as quoted by Theil): a rare contrastive downward glide occurs only on stressed syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone (lexical melodies over the whole word); Theil's realization statements refer to words before pause (citation/utterance-final context). The source is a one-page conference abstract by the describer; the full 2013 chapter and the 2011 JALL article were not accessible. Analyses conflict across authors (accent vs stress vs tone-accent vs pure word-tone), so a catalog entry should flag the disagreement.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Koorete proper (koor1239; also called Koyra/Badditu/Amarro; Hayward 1982 uses 'Koyra'). Theil's data: speakers from Amaaro-Keele and Addis Ababa, 2005-2007. Not to be confused with Koyra Chiini Songhay (koyr1240).

sources.note: Explicit: 'Koorete is not a stress or accent language. It has two distinctive word level tones, a rising tone and a falling tone' (minimal pairs given); rising = pitch rising through the word, last syllable L before pause; falling = slightly falling pitch through the word. Also summarizes Hayward 1982 (accentual, accent = heightened pitch) and Ford 1990 (loudness is the principal exponent of stress; rare contrastive falling glide only on stressed syllables).
